prompt.context: Your client is Whitesand Capital Partners, a large asset manager based in the US with $5 Trillion in Assets Under Management (AUM) and a presence in all large financial centers around the world. Whitesand was known for having some of the best talent in managing fixed income (bond) products in the past, and has been continually expanding its product offerings by acquiring other asset managers with different strengths. Despite AUM growth in both its Retail and Institutional customer segments, and being the largest asset manager in the world, Whitesand has recently been facing declining profitability and shareholders are demanding a shift in strategy. The CEO of Whitesand has brought you in to diagnose the problems and to help turn the firm's share price around.
prompt.question: What is causing Whitesand's declining profitability, and what should the firm do to reverse this trend?

clarifying_info.q: What is the goal or target for profitability improvement?
clarifying_info.a: The goal is simply to improve profitability; there is no specific number in mind.

clarifying_info.q: How does the company generate revenue?
clarifying_info.a: The company generates revenue by charging a fee on AUM managed. For example, 1% on $1 million AUM = $10,000 in revenue.

The two main segments are Retail and Institutional. Retail invests in simpler products like stocks and bonds. Institutional can invest in any kind of product. Retail and Institutional AUM is split 50/50, but the Institutional segment is growing faster.
Whitesand offers a range of traditional asset management products including Active and Passive products across Equities and Fixed Income, both US and International.

clarifying_info.q: What is the difference between Active and Passive products?
clarifying_info.a: Active products are more expensive because they employ people who try to outperform the market. Passive products simply mirror the market and do not outperform or underperform. Returns between passive and active classes are about the same.

clarifying_info.q: Which segment prefers which product type?
clarifying_info.a: The retail segment has a stronger appetite for lower-fee passive products, while the institutional segment is more likely to pay higher fees to try to get higher returns.

exhibits.title: Asset Class Expense Ratio (Basis Points, 1/100th of a Percent)
exhibits.shows: A bar chart comparing Whitesand's expense ratios (fees charged to clients) across eight asset classes — US Equity Active, US Equity Passive, US Fixed Income Active, US Fixed Income Passive, International Equity Active, International Equity Passive, International Fixed Income Active, International Fixed Income Passive — for the years 2016, 2018, and 2020. Active products carry higher basis-point fees than passive equivalents.
exhibits.data: Expense ratios shown in basis points (1 bp = 0.01%). All eight asset classes show declining fee trends from 2016 to 2020. Active products (US Equity Active ~120 bp in 2016 declining toward ~90 bp by 2020) carry materially higher fees than passive equivalents (US Equity Passive ~20 bp declining further). The note states: Expense Ratio = fee paid by client to Whitesand on each dollar of assets managed.

exhibits.title: Private Equity Index Returns (Yearly, %)
exhibits.shows: A bar chart of yearly returns (%) for four Private Equity fund types — Leveraged Buyout, Distressed Debt, Growth, and Venture Capital — across the years 2016, 2018, and 2020. The formula for total PE fees is shown: Total Fees = Management Fee * AUM + Performance Fee * AUM * (Return - Hurdle Rate).
exhibits.data: Leveraged Buyout returns: 13% (2016), 15% (2018), 14% (2020). Distressed Debt returns: 11% (2016), 9% (2018), 17% (2020). Growth returns: 13% (2016), 11% (2018), 14% (2020). Venture Capital returns: 23% (2016), 6% (2018), 14% (2020). Formula shown: Total Fees = Management Fee * AUM + Performance Fee * AUM * (Return - Hurdle Rate). Private Equity uses a 2/20 model: 2% management fee on capital invested, 20% performance fee on returns above the hurdle rate.

framework: Revenue: fee rate (expense ratio) x AUM — examine fee compression trends by product and segment
Costs: fixed (headcount, technology, facilities) vs. variable (trading, sourcing) — note Whitesand's scale advantage
Revenue diagnosis: use Exhibit 1 to identify which products/segments drive fee compression
Market entry angle: explore whether new, higher-fee products (e.g., Private Equity) can restore revenue growth
Segment lens: distinguish Retail vs. Institutional appetite — Institutional can access alternative products and is growing faster
Competitive landscape: assess whether fee compression is industry-wide and whether active management justifies its premium
Execution considerations for new product: talent, acquisitions, start-up costs, competition, brand fit

questions.prompt: What insights do you draw from Exhibit 1?
questions.guidance: Candidate should observe: (1) fee compression (declining expense ratios) across ALL eight asset classes from 2016 to 2020; (2) Active products carry higher fees than Passive equivalents in every category; (3) since active and passive returns are roughly the same, investors are rationally migrating from higher-fee active products to lower-fee passive ones; (4) this fee migration is the primary driver of revenue decline even as AUM grows; (5) a great candidate connects this to the Retail segment's preference for passive and asks whether there is a way to serve the higher-fee Institutional segment differently.

questions.prompt: Given the revenue trend, what could Whitesand do to reverse declining profitability? How would you evaluate entering the Private Equity market?
questions.guidance: Candidate should propose higher-fee product expansion, most naturally Private Equity. They should consider: (1) PE fees are materially higher than traditional products; (2) Institutional investors (the faster-growing segment) are eligible to invest in PE; (3) start-up costs include talent acquisition or firm acquisition; (4) competitive dynamics in PE; (5) brand/capability fit. After surfacing PE, hand Exhibit 2 and ask them to calculate fees for each fund type.

questions.prompt: Using Exhibit 2, calculate the total fees Whitesand would earn from each Private Equity fund type, assuming a 7% hurdle rate and $3 billion in invested capital per fund. Use the three data points for each fund type to extrapolate an average return.
questions.guidance: Candidate must apply the 2/20 model: Management Fee = 2% x AUM; Variable Fee = 20% x AUM x (Average Return - Hurdle Rate). They should average the three annual return data points for each fund type, then compute both fee components and sum them.

math.setup: 2/20 model: Management Fee = 2% x $3B = $60M for all funds. Variable Fee = 20% x $3B x (Avg Return - 7% hurdle). Total Fees = $60M + Variable Fee.
steps: Leveraged Buyout avg return = (13%+15%+14%)/3 = 14.0%. Variable Fee = $3B x (14%-7%) x 20% = $3B x 7% x 20% = $42M. Total = $60M + $42M = $102M.
Distressed Debt avg return = (11%+9%+17%)/3 = 12.3%. Variable Fee = $3B x (12.3%-7%) x 20% = $3B x 5.3% x 20% = $31.8M. Total = $60M + $31.8M = $91.8M.
Venture Capital avg return = (23%+6%+14%)/3 = 14.3%. Variable Fee = $3B x (14.3%-7%) x 20% = $3B x 7.3% x 20% = $43.8M. Total = $60M + $43.8M = $103.8M.
math.answer: LBO: $102M | Distressed Debt: $91.8M | Growth: $93.6M | Venture Capital: $103.8M (highest). Venture Capital and LBO generate the most total fees at comparable invested capital.

questions.prompt: Beyond the fee calculations, what other factors should Whitesand consider when deciding which type of Private Equity fund to launch?
questions.guidance: Strong answers include: (1) Return volatility — Venture Capital has the highest average but also the most volatile returns (23%, 6%, 14%), meaning variable fees could be zero in bad years; (2) Fund size — minimum commitments and market sizing differ by PE type; (3) Start-up costs — talent is scarce and expensive; may require acquiring a PE firm; (4) Competition — existing incumbents in each PE segment have deep track records; (5) Investor allocation constraints — how much of Institutional AUM is already allocated to PE; (6) Brand fit — does PE align with Whitesand's fixed-income/traditional heritage?

brainstorming.prompt: What other factors could Whitesand consider when deciding which type of Private Equity fund to start?

categories.name: Risk & Return Profile
ideas: Venture Capital has highest average return but highest volatility (range: 6%-23%), creating risk of zero variable fees
LBO returns are more stable (13%-15%), providing more predictable fee income
Distressed Debt has highest single-year return (17% in 2020) but lowest average

categories.name: Capability & Talent
ideas: PE requires specialist deal-sourcing, due diligence, and portfolio management talent
May require acquiring an existing PE firm to obtain track record and team
Whitesand's existing fixed income expertise is most adjacent to Distressed Debt

categories.name: Market & Competition
ideas: PE market is highly competitive with entrenched incumbents (Blackstone, KKR, Apollo)
Institutional LP market has existing PE relationships and allocation limits
Emerging managers face fundraising hurdles without track record

categories.name: Client & Segment Fit
ideas: Institutional investors are growing faster and can access PE — natural fit
Retail investors cannot invest in PE (regulatory restrictions)
Whitesand's institutional relationships are an advantage for distribution

categories.name: Strategic Fit & Brand
ideas: PE is operationally very different from public markets asset management
Integration risk if acquiring a PE firm
Brand extension from traditional asset manager to alternatives requires careful positioning

recommendation: Whitesand Capital Partners should enter the Private Equity market, most likely via Leveraged Buyout given the best balance of fee generation ($102M per $3B AUM) and return stability.
Venture Capital could also be considered for higher potential fees ($103.8M) but carries significant return volatility that would compress variable fee income in down years.
risks: Traditional product fee compression will continue regardless of PE entry — needs parallel cost management
Venture Capital variable fees are at risk in low-return years (e.g., 2018: only 6% return, below or near hurdle)
PE market entry requires significant upfront investment in talent or M&A, with uncertain payback period
Institutional investors may already have full PE allocations, limiting near-term capital capture
Integration of a PE business culture into a large traditional asset manager is organizationally complex
next_steps: Assess whether to build or acquire a PE capability (acqui-hire of boutique PE firm is faster but costly)
Conduct institutional investor survey to gauge PE allocation headroom and appetite
Model full P&L impact including PE start-up costs against projected fee uplift over 3-5 year horizon
Define which PE sub-strategy to lead with based on talent availability and competitive positioning
Develop investor relations strategy to communicate the strategic pivot to current shareholders
